items.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: The saxophones were Marshall Royal, Frank Wess, Ernie Wilkins, Charlie Fowlkes on baritone, and myself.

ctx.x: When you joined the band who was there at that point?

In the trumpet section were Joe Newman, a gentleman by the name of Paul Campbell -- they used to call him Uncle Cam -- Wendell Culley, a very distinguished looking and acting person from Worchester, Mass., who spoke perfect English and was a gentleman and always wore a suit and tie. I said Joe Newman, right? The lead trumpeter was a person called Renauld Jones. Trombones were Henry Coker, Benny Powell, and the composer-arranger Johnny Mandel. The saxophones were Marshall Royal, Frank Wess, Ernie Wilkins, Charlie…
So at that point Jimmy Wilkins had left the band?

items.title: Frank Foster interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 7, 1998
items.q: the saxophone section at that time was excellent with Marshall Royal playing lead... I fit into the section very well

ctx.x: Did you go through a period of trying to adjust your style, or feel that you needed to adjust your style to play what was required or to fit the Basie band and still satisfy your need for bop?

items.title: 52222_Marshall Royal oral history interview
items.q: In the early years in the Basie Band... we got a young dude out of the service by the name of Frank Foster... Frank West was an excellent arranger

ctx.x: Yes. Who was doing most of the -- you had several top arrangers during those years?

In the early years in the Basie Band, we had probably the best jazz arrangers in the business. Ernie Wilkins in a premier arranger of jazz. Then we got a young dude out of the service by the name of Frank Foster and he was

a young genius. He could arrange anything of any mood, if you would just tie him down long enough. Frank West was an excellent arranger, although he did very little in the band. He was an excellent arranger. Then Thad Jones came into the band and he was a monster. He was latter-day Duke Ellington type arranger. That is the way that I feel.

items.title: Frank Foster and Bill Hughes interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Schenectady, New York, March 28, 1995
items.q: And with Joe Williams and Sonny Payne there too, and Marshall Royal playing lead alto... I mean he was, see the voice of the band was Marshall Royal

ctx.x: It wasn’t as polished as the band in the late 50’s.

Right. We developed into a precision, a slick, precision, east coast jazz machine. But still, lots of feeling, the feeling never left. So the precision and the polish came, and the feeling, you know it just steamrolled over people. And with Joe Williams and Sonny Payne there too, and Marshall Royal playing lead alto, I mean he was, see the voice of the band was Marshall Royal, Snooky Young and Henry Coker, the lead players. And together they gave the band one hell-fired voice.
Yes they did. You’re making me cry for it.
